gates.name: Accumulation
gates.question: Can we collect, store and retrieve the data?

gates.name: Accessibility
gates.question: Can authorised people find and use it?

gates.name: Interpretation
gates.question: Do we agree on what it means and what it can support?

gates.name: Assurance
gates.question: Can we challenge, reproduce and defend the insight?

gates.name: Consequence
gates.question: Did the insight change action and improve an outcome?

questions.prompt: A leader asks for last quarter's figures for a strategically important customer segment.

options.text: Nobody holds them in one place; they have to be rebuilt from team spreadsheets.
The data is in the warehouse, but a whole channel, region or product line is missing and nobody has written that down.
It is collected and stored centrally, and we know roughly what is and is not covered.
Collected, stored and retrievable, with coverage gaps documented and visible to whoever uses it.

questions.prompt: An analyst in another function needs that data for a legitimate purpose.

options.text: They ask a colleague who has a copy. Access follows who you know.
They raise a ticket and wait weeks for access.
They find it in a catalogue and get access through a set route, though nobody checks what it will be used for.
They find it, see who owns it, and get access for their stated purpose through self-service.

questions.prompt: Two functions present churn in the same meeting, and the numbers differ.

options.text: The meeting argues about which number is right and ends by asking for another report.
Everyone knows the definitions differ; the difference is explained aloud each time and never written down.
Decision-critical terms have a written definition and an owner, but approved variants and historical meanings are lost when one canonical definition is imposed.
Each term has an owner, a recorded history and a clear scope; disagreement is visible and treated as evidence.

questions.prompt: Before analysis begins on a consequential decision, someone asks what this data can actually support.

options.text: Nobody asks. Analysis starts from whatever data is available, and the question is shaped to fit it.
The question is named, but nobody states what kind of claim it needs or what evidence would settle it.
Decision, question and type of claim are written down, with the population, period and exclusions defined.
All of that, and someone checks the data can answer the question before work starts; claims it cannot support are labelled.

questions.prompt: A board member asks how a headline number in the pack was produced.

options.text: The presenter cannot say. The number came from a dashboard, and the dashboard came from somewhere.
An analyst could reconstruct it in a day or two by retracing spreadsheets and queries.
Source, definition, time window and transformation are documented; reproduction is possible but manual.
The claim links to its source, method, version and approval, and can be replayed as it stood at decision time.

questions.prompt: The preferred explanation is on the table and the room is ready to move.

options.text: One narrative is presented as self-evident. Raising a counter-story would be read as opposition.
Someone may play devil's advocate informally, but nobody owns the challenge and it leaves no record.
A plausible counter-story is written down for major decisions, but rarely tested against evidence.
The strongest counter-story is named, linked to a test that could tell the two apart, and its outcome recorded before commitment.

questions.prompt: A forecast with real uncertainty goes to the person who must decide.

options.text: It arrives as a single number, with no caveats and no date; confidence is expressed as tone.
The caveats sit in a footnote or appendix the decision-maker never reads.
What is estimated, incomplete or contested is stated, but collapsed into one score or a traffic light.
What was observed, inferred, projected and unknown is shown separately, in a form the decision-maker can act on.

questions.prompt: An insight is accepted. What happens on Monday?

options.text: Nothing specific. The insight is noted, the deck is filed, and people return to existing plans.
Someone acts on it, but the action drifts beyond what was agreed.
A named owner takes the action with a deadline; scope, stop conditions and rollback are informal.
Action, owner, scope, what it will never do and who can stop it are written down before it starts.

questions.prompt: Six months after the decision, what does the organisation know about its effect?

options.text: Whether it happened. Success is measured by delivery, dashboard views or adoption, not outcomes.
The headline metric improved and success was declared; nobody checked who lost out.
Outcomes are reviewed against a baseline for major decisions, but findings rarely change the next question.
Consequences are observed across groups and over time, attributed honestly, and used to update definitions, questions and standards.

levels.name: Accumulation
levels.verdict: Your enterprise is collecting data it cannot yet rely on. Coverage is patchy, and a current, complete version of a key figure still has to be assembled by hand. Every later capability depends on this level, and the fix is not another warehouse.
levels.symptom: Every leadership meeting ends by asking for more data, and the most trusted copy of the numbers lives in someone's spreadsheet.
levels.challenge: What if the archive keeps growing because no one has named a decision it must answer?

chapters.why: Name the decision before the dataset.
What kind of truth this data can support, and what lies outside its view.
Authorised, minimum-necessary access to a shared picture.

levels.capability: Divya Drishti Engine, with Sanjaya Lens
levels.cta: Put one decision at the centre of your data.

levels.name: Accessibility
levels.verdict: People can find the data. They do not agree on what it means. The dashboards multiply, the same metric carries three values, and the room debates which is right instead of what to do.
levels.symptom: A red indicator that could mean deterioration, a definition change, a delayed feed or a seasonal pattern, and nobody can say which.
levels.challenge: What if the functions disagree not because a shared definition is missing, but because each is rewarded for defending its own number?

chapters.why: A dashboard is a view, not a verdict.
Recovering shared meaning, provenance and history.
Asking the question that fits the decision.

levels.name: Interpretation
levels.verdict: Your enterprise agrees what its numbers mean, and Project EPIC begins here. What it cannot yet do is say how a claim was produced, what would have to be true for it to be wrong, or how much confidence the evidence warrants. Insights are believed on presentation, not on assurance.
levels.symptom: The pack is fluent, the counter-story is unwritten, and confidence rests on who presented it.
levels.challenge: Which decision in the last year was accepted because nobody felt safe enough to challenge it?

chapters.why: Testing whether a decision survives being wrong.
The Nine Gates a claim must pass before anyone acts on it.
Reconstructing what was known and authorised.

levels.name: Assurance
levels.verdict: Insights are challenged, traceable and honestly qualified. Then they stop. Either nothing follows, or something follows, drifts beyond its authority and is never measured. The enterprise is trustworthy in analysis and unaccountable in action.
levels.symptom: The action shipped on time, the dashboard turned green, and nobody can say who was worse off.
levels.challenge: If the intervention shifted harm onto a smaller group, would anyone in the organisation be responsible for noticing?

chapters.why: An action contract with an owner, bounds and a way to stop.
Did it create durable value, and for whom?
Coordinating systems so the whole action stays legitimate.

levels.name: Consequence
levels.verdict: Consequences return to governance and change the next question. Few enterprises reach this honestly, so treat the result as a claim to test. The remaining risk is the language of the framework spreading faster than the capability behind it.
levels.symptom: The framework's name appears in board decks before a second domain has run a full cycle.
levels.challenge: Could the framework itself be retired responsibly, or has it become the thing nobody may challenge?

chapters.why: Building the capability without framework theatre.
Allocating judgement between people and machines.

levels.capability: Building the EPIC Enterprise, with the Sarathi Reasoner
